Exact Conditional Poisson Regression: Theory and Implementation

Source: vignettes/Theory-Implementation.Rmd
Theory-Implementation.Rmd

This document explains the theory behind every exact-inference algorithm in this package:

  • ep_closed_form(): a fast, closed-form method for the special case of one two-level effect with strata as the only other structure.
  • ep_multi_shift(): a general method that allows any number of categorical covariates and strata.
  • ep_network(): a general method that computes the same mathematics again, using a different strategy that prunes more aggressively.

All three are independently implemented, yet compute exactly the same conditional distribution; this document derives why that is true, and works through exactly how each of the three arrives at it.

For a worked, runnable example that puts this theory to use, such as simulating a low-incidence vaccine-efficacy trial, comparing the package’s exact inference against glm()’s asymptotic inference, and reusing an already-computed exact distribution to answer a different question without recomputing it, see the companion vignette, vignette("Example").

1. Motivation: why exact conditional inference

Poisson regression with a log link is the standard way to model counts and event rates. The usual way of testing hypotheses and building confidence intervals for it (Wald tests, likelihood-ratio tests, asymptotic confidence intervals) relies on large-sample approximations. These approximations describe what happens as the sample size grows very large, and they can be poor when:

  • sample sizes are small,
  • the outcome is a rare event,
  • the model has many categorical levels or many strata, each with few events,
  • an estimated rate ratio is close to the edge of what the data can tell apart from zero or infinity (quasi-complete separation).

Exact conditional inference avoids large-sample approximations entirely. Instead of relying on how an estimator behaves as the sample grows, it builds the exact distribution of a test statistic for the sample size actually observed. It does this by eliminating every nuisance parameter through conditioning on that parameter’s sufficient statistic. Every p-value, confidence interval, and point estimate this produces is exact, not an approximation. This is the same idea behind Fisher’s exact test for 2x2 tables and exact logistic regression (Cox 1970; Hirji, Mehta and Patel 1987; Mehta and Patel 1995).

This document works through the same idea for the Poisson case. Section 3 first states the general principle it rests on. Sections 5 through 7 then describe three algorithms that compute it: one fully general algorithm (Section 5), one restricted to an important special case where a closed form is available (Section 6), and one more that computes the same general-case answer as Section 5, but by a different, more aggressively pruned route (Section 7).

2. The model and notation shared by every algorithm

2.1 Indices and strata

Let i \in \{1,\dots,n\} index the observations. Observations can optionally be split into Q disjoint strata, I_s \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}, \qquad I_s \cap I_{s'} = \varnothing \ (s \ne s'), \qquad \bigcup_{s=1}^Q I_s = \{1,\dots,n\}. Write s(i) for the stratum that contains observation i. If no stratification variable is supplied, Q = 1 and every observation belongs to one pseudo-stratum called “ALL.” Because of this convention, every statement below about “strata” also covers the unstratified case, and neither the code nor this document needs a special case for it.

2.2 Response, offset, exposure

The observed response is a vector of non-negative integer counts y^{\mathrm{obs}} = (y_1^{\mathrm{obs}}, \dots, y_n^{\mathrm{obs}}). An optional offset o_i \in \mathbb{R} (a log-exposure) defines the exposure E_i := \exp(o_i) > 0. If no offset is supplied, every function in this package sets o_i = 0 and E_i = 1 for every observation (one unit of exposure each), so an unspecified offset never needs special handling later.

2.3 Design: the interest column and the nuisance columns

Every algorithm in this package does exact inference for one scalar coefficient at a time. (The general algorithms can repeat this for several requested effects, one after another.)

Notation convention used from here on. A bold letter denotes a vector or matrix; the same letter in ordinary (non-bold) type denotes a single scalar entry of it, normally picked out by a subscript. For example \mathbf{z} = (z_1,\dots,z_n) is the whole interest column and z_i is its i-th entry; \boldsymbol{\gamma} = (\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_p) is the whole nuisance coefficient vector and \gamma_k is its k-th entry. The handful of quantities that are conventionally written as plain (non-bold) letters even though they collect several numbers (\tau = (\tau_1,\dots,\tau_Q), the vector of stratum intercepts, and \theta,\beta,\lambda_s, which are always scalars) follow the established convention of the literature this document cites (Guess and Thomas 1990; Hirji, Mehta and Patel 1987) rather than this rule, and are called out individually wherever they first appear.

  • \mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{Z}^n is the interest design column, with i-th entry z_i, typically a 0/1 dummy for one level of a categorical effect. Its coefficient \beta is the target of inference.
  • X_N \in \mathbb{Z}^{n \times p} is the nuisance design matrix (“N” for “nuisance,” to distinguish it from the sample size n): every other model effect that is not currently being tested, collected as columns. This can include other categorical covariates, as well as other dummy columns of the same multi-level factor that \mathbf{z} belongs to. Row i of X_N, written \mathbf{x}_{N,i} \in \mathbb{Z}^p, is the nuisance-column values for observation i; its k-th entry is x_{N,i,k}. The nuisance coefficient vector paired with X_N is \boldsymbol{\gamma} \in \mathbb{R}^p.

Scope: categorical effects only. Both \mathbf{z} and every column of X_N must be small-integer-valued: concretely, values in \{0,1,\dots,K\} for some small K, almost always K=1 (a 0/1 dummy). In practice this means the 0/1 dummy columns produced by treatment-coding a categorical factor (Sections 5.1 and 6.1 give the exact details). The dynamic program, convolution, and network recursion in Sections 5-7 all work by explicitly listing every value a column can take, one at a time; their cost grows with the number of distinct values (roughly linearly per nuisance coordinate, and multiplicatively across coordinates for the joint table of Section 3.4). A handful of categorical levels (the ordinary case: a handful of treatment arms or a handful of ordered bins) keeps this listing cheap. This implementation does not support continuous covariates (for example, a continuous biomarker, or age measured in years) as either the interest effect or an adjustment covariate. A continuous variable has to be converted to a categorical one first (grouped into a small number of ordered levels) before it can be used with any of these functions. Section 4.7 notes the caveat that comes with this: grouping a continuous covariate into bins throws away information compared to modelling it on its original scale.

2.4 The stratified Poisson log-linear model

Y_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_i), \qquad \mu_i = E_i\exp(\eta_i), \qquad \eta_i = \tau_{s(i)} + \beta z_i + \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{x}_{N,i}, equivalently \log \mu_i = o_i + \tau_{s(i)} + \beta z_i + \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{x}_{N,i}. \qquad\text{(2.1)} \tau_{s(i)} is not a separate intercept for each observation. It means “observation i uses the intercept that belongs to its own stratum s(i).” The full intercept vector \tau = (\tau_1,\dots,\tau_Q) has one entry per stratum. Every stratum has its own free parameter: there is no shared reference level, and no assumption that intercepts are related across strata in any way. This point matters a great deal in Section 4. Every nuisance quantity here (the Q stratum intercepts and the p nuisance coefficients) gets eliminated by conditioning, as explained next.

One modelling choice is easy to miss, because it is about what is absent from (2.1) rather than what is present: \beta itself carries no stratum index. It is one shared number, used identically for every observation no matter which stratum it falls in; it is not \beta_{s(i)}, the way \tau_{s(i)} is. This is the general version of an assumption that Guess and Thomas (1990) state explicitly for the two-group case handled by this package’s closed-form algorithm (Section 6.1): “the relative risk is assumed to be constant across strata.” Every algorithm in this package makes this same assumption for whichever effect is being tested, because every algorithm starts from the same model (2.1). It is not a simplification specific to the closed-form special case, and using the fully general multivariate-shift or network algorithms instead (Sections 5 and 7) does not relax it.

It is worth being precise about why giving every stratum its own free intercept \tau_s does not, by itself, relax this assumption. The two are separate, independent pieces of (2.1). \tau_s sets each stratum’s own baseline event rate at the reference level of every tested or adjusted effect, and is free to differ arbitrarily from one stratum to the next. \beta sets how much that rate changes when z_i changes, and (2.1) says that this change is the same number in every stratum, no matter how different their baselines are. Making the intercepts more flexible (more strata, a finer partition, even one intercept per observation) never touches \beta’s own single coefficient. It only changes how much nuisance structure gets conditioned away (Section 3). A model can have arbitrarily many, arbitrarily different stratum baselines and still assume one constant effect on top of them: that is exactly what (2.1) specifies. (This is the same “common effect” assumption used in Mantel-Haenszel-type common-odds-ratio estimation and in proportional-hazards models with stratified baselines. It is well established elsewhere and is not a limitation specific to this package.)

If a genuinely stratum-varying effect is wanted (for example, the rate ratio for \mathbf{z} differing by region), it has to be modelled explicitly, as an interaction between \mathbf{z} and the variable it is allowed to vary by. (exact_vars can name such an interaction directly; see Section 5’s discussion of interaction-term naming, and Section 4.3’s composite-variable construction, for how a term like this turns into model-matrix columns.) Doing so replaces the single \beta with one coefficient per level of the interacting variable. Each of those coefficients is then just another effect being tested under this package’s usual assumption: constant across whatever grouping remains once the interaction’s own levels are accounted for. There is no way to ask this package for a coefficient that is simultaneously “the effect of \mathbf{z}” and “different in every stratum” without naming that difference as its own term. Simply adding more strata never does it.

2.5 Notation at a glance, and one deliberate disambiguation

Several symbols below carry more than one index. It is worth fixing, once and for all, which quantities are single numbers per stratum and which are numbers per stratum and per nuisance coordinate, because two of them are easy to mix up at a glance:

Symbol Meaning Indexed by
M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} The observed total count of stratum s, \sum_{i\in I_s} y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}. This is the one number each stratum’s intercept gets conditioned on. stratum s only, one number per stratum.
\mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}} The observed nuisance statistic vector, X_N^\top y^{\mathrm{obs}} (Section 2.3) nuisance coordinate k=1,\dots,p only, shared across every stratum, not stratum-specific
S_i The per-observation cap on y_i (Section 5.2) observation i only
U_{s,k} The most stratum s could possibly contribute to nuisance coordinate k, given only its own observations and its own total M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} (defined in Section 5.5) both stratum s and coordinate k
L_{s,k} The least stratum s could possibly be forced to contribute to nuisance coordinate k (defined in Section 5.5; used only by the network algorithm, Section 7) both stratum s and coordinate k

Here is why this table is worth spelling out. U_{s,k} and L_{s,k} are each defined as a min/max expression with M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} as one of its two arguments (Section 5.5 gives the equation for U_{s,k}). So M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} appears inside a formula indexed by k, without itself depending on k. Read out of context, a formula like “U_{s,k} = \min(M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}, \dots)” can look as though M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} has picked up a k subscript it does not actually have. It has not. M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} is always the same single number for every k within stratum s (the stratum’s own observed total, exactly as defined in Section 2.4), and it only ever plays the role of one candidate value inside a \min or \max whose other candidate value depends on k (a sum of S_i over a subset of observations that depends on k). Every formula in this document that mixes M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} with a k-indexed quantity should be read this way: one plain scalar meeting one per-coordinate quantity, not a hidden second family of “M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} values.” Sections 5.5 and 7 use the same pair of symbols, U_{s,k} and L_{s,k}, throughout for exactly this reason, rather than re-deriving and renaming the same quantity elsewhere.

3. The general principle: exponential families and eliminating nuisance parameters by conditioning

The Poisson-specific derivations in Sections 5-7 are all examples of one classical fact about exponential families that holds for any model, not just Poisson models. Stating that fact first, in general terms, makes clear that “eliminate nuisance parameters by conditioning on their sufficient statistics” is not a Poisson-specific trick, and is not specific to any one of the three algorithms. All three compute the same conditional distribution, just by different routes. This section also fixes the vocabulary (“canonical parameter”, “canonical sufficient statistic”) used for the rest of the document.

3.1 The model as a canonical exponential family

The Poisson log-likelihood for model (2.1) is \begin{aligned} \ell(\tau,\beta,\boldsymbol{\gamma}) &= \sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i\log\mu_i - \mu_i - \log(y_i!)\big) \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^n y_i\big(o_i+\tau_{s(i)}+\beta z_i+\boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{x}_{N,i}\big) \;-\; \sum_{i=1}^n \mu_i \;-\;\sum_{i=1}^n \log(y_i!). \end{aligned} Collect the terms that are linear in y_i, grouped by which parameter they multiply: \ell(\tau,\beta,\boldsymbol{\gamma}) = \underbrace{\sum_{s=1}^Q \tau_s M_s(y)}_{\text{stratum intercepts}} \;+\; \underbrace{\beta\, T(y)}_{\text{interest}} \;+\; \underbrace{\boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{T}_N(y)}_{\text{nuisance covariates}} \;-\; \sum_i \mu_i \;+\; \log w(y), \qquad\text{(3.1)} Here M_s(y) := \sum_{i\in I_s} y_i, T(y) := \sum_i y_i z_i, \mathbf{T}_N(y) := X_N^\top y, and w(y) := \prod_i E_i^{y_i}/y_i! is the Poisson base measure. (Section 5.1 spells out every algebraic step of this same factorization, for anyone who wants to see it in full.) Equation (3.1) is exactly the canonical form of a multi-parameter exponential family: a linear combination of canonical parameters (\tau_1,\dots,\tau_Q,\beta,\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_p) against their canonical sufficient statistics (M_1,\dots,M_Q,T,\mathbf{T}_N), plus a normalizing term and a base measure that do not depend on the parameters.

3.2 The conditioning theorem

Here is the general fact. Take a canonical exponential family, and split its canonical parameter into a target piece and a nuisance piece. The conditional distribution of the data, given the sufficient statistic of the nuisance piece alone, no longer depends on the nuisance parameters at all. It depends only on the target parameter, in the usual tilted form. This is a standard result in the theory of exponential families (Lehmann and Romano 2005, ch. 2 and ch. 4; Andersen 1970; Cox 1970; see also Agresti 2013, ch. 6-7, for its use with nuisance intercepts in categorical/count data). Applied to (3.1), with (\tau,\boldsymbol{\gamma}) as the nuisance piece and \beta as the target, it says: \Pr\nolimits_{\tau,\beta,\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\big(Y=y \ \big|\ M_s(Y)=M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}\ \forall s,\ \ \mathbf{T}_N(Y)=\mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}}\big) \ \ \text{does not depend on } (\tau,\boldsymbol{\gamma}). \qquad\text{(3.2)} This is why conditioning works in general, not only for this particular model and not only for one of the three algorithms below. It follows directly from (3.1) being in canonical exponential-family form. It does not need to be re-checked by hand every time a new nuisance structure is added, or a new algorithm is written to compute it. What is specific to the Poisson distribution is that the resulting conditional distribution turns out to have a convenient, explicitly computable form: a base-measure-weighted count over a combinatorial reference set (Section 3.4). That convenience is what the rest of this document uses computationally. But the validity of conditioning itself follows from (3.1) alone, with nothing Poisson-specific about it.

3.3 Finite conditional reference sets

Poisson counts are unbounded, so turning (3.2) into something we can actually sum over requires a finite sample space, made explicit. Introduce per-observation caps S_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}, with 0 \le y_i \le S_i (Section 5.2 gives the exact rules used to set them, together with a short proof of which are forced by conditioning alone and which are extra modelling choices; see in particular the paragraph beginning “Rule 2’s cap is implied by conditioning alone,” which derives that claim directly from the stratum-total conditioning event itself, with nothing further assumed). Define the cap box \mathcal{B}(Q) := \{\, y \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^n : 0 \le y_i \le S_i\ \forall i \,\}. The intercept-conditioned feasible set and the fully conditioned set are \Omega := \Big\{\, y \in \mathcal{B}(Q) : \sum_{i \in I_s} y_i = M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}\ \ \forall s \,\Big\}, \qquad \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}} := \{\, y \in \Omega : X_N^\top y = \mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}} \,\}. For any statistic value t and nuisance value \mathbf{c}, the fibers (the sets of allocations that achieve exactly those values) are \Omega(t,\mathbf{c}) := \{\, y \in \Omega : T(y)=t,\ X_N^\top y = \mathbf{c} \,\}, \qquad \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}(t) := \{\, y \in \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}} : T(y) = t \,\}.

3.4 Coefficient tables and the conditional law of T

This section derives (3.3) below step by step from (3.1)-(3.2), rather than only stating the result, because “collecting like terms into a coefficient table” is exactly what every algorithm in Sections 5-7 computes. They differ only in the bookkeeping strategy used to do it, never in the target itself.

Step 1: why \tau and \boldsymbol{\gamma} drop out of the conditional probability, concretely. By definition, conditioning restricts attention to y \in \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}} and renormalizes: \begin{aligned} \Pr\nolimits_{\tau,\beta,\boldsymbol{\gamma}}(Y=y \mid Y \in \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}) = \frac{\Pr\nolimits_{\tau,\beta,\boldsymbol{\gamma}}(Y=y)}{\sum_{y' \in \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}} \Pr\nolimits_{\tau,\beta,\boldsymbol{\gamma}}(Y=y')}, \qquad y \in \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}. \end{aligned} From the canonical form (3.1), \Pr_{\tau,\beta,\boldsymbol{\gamma}}(Y=y) \propto \exp\!\big(\sum_s \tau_s M_s(y) + \beta T(y) + \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{T}_N(y)\big)\, w(y). The term -\sum_i \mu_i from (3.1) has already been absorbed into this “\propto,” and it is worth saying explicitly why, since the reason is more basic than the argument given below for \tau and \boldsymbol{\gamma}. Unlike M_s(y), T(y), and \mathbf{T}_N(y), the quantity \mu_i = E_i\exp(\tau_{s(i)}+\beta z_i+\boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{x}_{N,i}) does not depend on y at all; it is a function only of the parameters and the fixed design and offsets. So once (\tau,\beta,\boldsymbol{\gamma}) are held fixed, \sum_i \mu_i is a single number, the same for every candidate y in the entire sample space, not merely for y \in \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}. The factor e^{-\sum_i\mu_i} therefore multiplies \Pr(Y=y) by an identical constant no matter which y is plugged in, so it cancels top and bottom in any ratio of probabilities and can be dropped the instant two probabilities are compared, which is exactly what “\propto” records here. (In exponential-family language, \sum_i\mu_i is the log-partition function of the canonical form (3.1): the piece that depends on the parameters alone and never on the data. It always drops out of statements about the shape of the distribution across y, with or without any conditioning.) Now look at the \tau and \boldsymbol{\gamma} terms for y ranging over \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}. By the definition of \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}} (Section 3.3), every y in this set satisfies M_s(y) = M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} for all s, and \mathbf{T}_N(y) = \mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}}. So \sum_s \tau_s M_s(y) = \sum_s \tau_s M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} and \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{T}_N(y) = \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}} take the same value for every single y in \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}. They never distinguish one member of \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}} from another. A factor that is constant across every term of both the numerator and the denominator of a ratio cancels exactly: \begin{aligned} \Pr\nolimits_\beta(Y=y \mid Y \in \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}) &= \frac{e^{\sum_s \tau_s M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} + \beta T(y) + \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top\mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}}}\, w(y)}{\sum_{y'\in\Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}} e^{\sum_s \tau_s M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} + \beta T(y') + \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top\mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}}}\, w(y')} \\ &= \frac{e^{\beta T(y)}\, w(y)}{\sum_{y'\in\Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}} e^{\beta T(y')}\, w(y')} \ \propto\ w(y)\, e^{\beta T(y)}. \end{aligned} \qquad\text{(3.3a)} This makes (3.2) concrete rather than merely asserted: \tau and \boldsymbol{\gamma} vanish because conditioning pins their canonical sufficient statistics to one exact value, shared by every allocation still under consideration. Only \beta survives in the conditional distribution, because its statistic T(y) genuinely differs from one y \in \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}} to another.

Step 2: grouping allocations by the value of T. We ultimately want the distribution of the scalar T(Y), not the distribution of the full vector Y. Many different allocations y can share the same value of T(y), so partition \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}} into fibers \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}(t): the set of allocations that all give the same value T(y)=t (Section 3.3). Inside one fiber, the factor e^{\beta T(y)} = e^{\beta t} in (3.3a) is identical for every member, so it can be pulled out of the sum over that fiber: \Pr\nolimits_\beta(T=t \mid Y\in\Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}) = \sum_{y \in \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}(t)} \Pr\nolimits_\beta(Y=y\mid Y\in\Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}) \ \propto\ e^{\beta t} \sum_{y \in \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}(t)} w(y). Define the coefficient table as exactly that inner sum: add up the base-measure weight of every allocation that produces this particular value of t: C(t) := \sum_{y \in \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}(t)} w(y). For example, suppose t=3 happens to be achievable by exactly two allocations, y^{(1)} and y^{(2)}, with base-measure weights w(y^{(1)}) and w(y^{(2)}). Then C(3) = w(y^{(1)}) + w(y^{(2)}): nothing more than collecting like terms. C(t) is precisely the coefficient of e^{\beta t} once every allocation’s contribution w(y)e^{\beta T(y)} has been grouped by its exponent t; see Section 6.3 for further details, where this same idea is made completely literal: the closed-form algorithm’s own coefficient table is, quite concretely, the coefficient of a power of a single polynomial variable.

Step 3: the joint table C(t,\mathbf{c}), and why it gets computed first. \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}} additionally requires \mathbf{T}_N(y) = \mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}} exactly. This constraint is awkward to enumerate directly, since it depends on which nuisance total actually happened to be observed. It is far more convenient to enumerate over the larger, easier-to-describe set \Omega instead (only the stratum-total constraints, no nuisance constraint yet; Section 3.3), grouping allocations by both T(y)=t and \mathbf{T}_N(y)=\mathbf{c} at once: C(t,\mathbf{c}) := \sum_{y \in \Omega(t,\mathbf{c})} w(y). C(t) is then just one slice of this finer table, at the observed nuisance value: C(t) = C(t,\mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}}), since \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}(t) = \Omega(t,\mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}}) follows directly from the definition of \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}. This is exactly why Sections 5 and 7 build the two-dimensional-in-(t,\mathbf{c}) table first (by dynamic programming and convolution, or by a network with continuous pruning), and only afterwards filter down to \mathbf{c}=\mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}} and drop the \mathbf{c} key (Section 5.6, “filtering and marginalizing”). Both algorithms enumerate over the convenient set \Omega the whole time, and only narrow down to \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}} at the very last step (or, for the network algorithm, gradually before it).

Step 4: the conditional pmf of T. Normalizing Step 2’s proportionality (dividing by the same sum over every attainable t) gives the exponential-tilt form used throughout the rest of this document: \begin{aligned} p_\beta(t) \;=\; \Pr\nolimits_\beta\big(T=t \mid \mathbf{T}_N = \mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}}, \{M_s = M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}\}\big) \;&=\; \frac{C(t)\, e^{\beta t}}{\displaystyle\sum_{u \in \mathcal{T}} C(u)\, e^{\beta u}}, \\ \qquad \mathcal{T} :&= \{\,t : \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}(t) \ne \varnothing\,\}. \end{aligned} \qquad\text{(3.3)} Every downstream exact quantity (p-value, confidence interval, conditional maximum likelihood estimate, MLE) is a function of the one-dimensional table \{(t, C(t))\}_{t \in \mathcal{T}} alone (Section 8). (“Conditional” MLE because it maximizes the conditional likelihood p_\beta(t) of (3.3) just derived, not the ordinary, unconditional likelihood of Y; Section 8.2 gives the precise equation it solves.) The entire computational problem of exact conditional Poisson regression is therefore the problem of computing C(t) (equivalently, computing C(t,\mathbf{c}) and then slicing and marginalizing it, as in Step 3). The three algorithms in this package differ only in how they compute this table, never in what it means or in what is done with it once it is obtained.

4. Adjustment vs. stratification: when they agree, and when they don’t

Section 2.4 treats “strata” and “nuisance covariates to adjust for” as two visibly different mechanisms. Strata get their own free intercept \tau_s per level, with no dummy coding and no reference level. Adjustment covariates enter through \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{x}_{N,i}, with the usual reference-coded dummy columns. A natural question is whether these are truly different things, or the same thing computed two different ways. It is worth answering precisely, since the package’s API (the strata= argument versus adjusting for a variable in the formula) forces a choice, for every algorithm in this package equally.

The short answer: they give identical exact inference in one specific, narrow case (Sections 4.1-4.2), and that case generalizes cleanly to several variables stratified jointly, provided the adjustment side matches it term for term (Section 4.3). Trouble starts when it doesn’t: when a variable is added to an existing stratification as a plain adjustment covariate rather than as a further stratum. Section 4.4 walks through exactly why that produces different numbers, using a worked example. Section 4.7 then gives practical guidance, in a clinical-trials setting, for choosing between the two.

4.1 The narrow case where the two are the same model

Suppose G is a categorical variable with levels g=1,\dots,Q, and it is the only nuisance structure being considered, with nothing else in the model yet. Let its levels define the stratum partition, I_s := \{i : G_i = s\}. Compare:

  • Model A (stratify by G alone). \eta_i = \tau_{s(i)} + \beta z_i, with Q free stratum intercepts \tau_1,\dots,\tau_Q and no shared global intercept.
  • Model B (adjust for G alone). \eta_i = \tau_0 + \beta z_i + \delta^\top d_i, with a single global intercept \tau_0, and d_i \in \{0,1\}^{Q-1} the usual reference-coded dummy vector for G (level 1 dropped as reference), with free coefficient vector \delta \in \mathbb{R}^{Q-1}.

These are the same statistical model, just written with different labels for the same parameters. Setting \tau_0 := \tau_1 and \delta_g := \tau_g - \tau_1 for g=2,\dots,Q gives \eta_i^{(A)} = \eta_i^{(B)} for every observation and every value of the free parameters. The map (\tau_1,\dots,\tau_Q) \leftrightarrow (\tau_0,\delta_2,\dots,\delta_Q) is an invertible linear change of variables from \mathbb{R}^Q to \mathbb{R}^Q. So Model A and Model B produce exactly the same set of possible linear predictors, and therefore exactly the same likelihood as a function of the data.

4.2 The two conditioning events are the same event

Model A’s canonical sufficient statistics for its nuisance parameters (\tau_1,\dots,\tau_Q) are the stratum totals (M_1,\dots,M_Q) (Section 3.1). Model B’s canonical sufficient statistics for its nuisance parameters (\tau_0,\delta_2,\dots,\delta_Q) are \big(M_{\mathrm{total}},\, T_{N,2},\dots,T_{N,Q}\big), where M_{\mathrm{total}} := \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i and T_{N,g} := \sum_i Y_i\, d_{i,g} = \sum_{i \in I_g} Y_i = M_g (since d_{i,g}=1 exactly when G_i=g). So Model B’s statistic vector is (M_{\mathrm{total}}, M_2,\dots,M_Q) = \big(\textstyle\sum_{s=1}^Q M_s,\ M_2,\dots,M_Q\big): an invertible linear function of Model A’s (M_1,\dots,M_Q), since M_1 = M_{\mathrm{total}} - \sum_{g=2}^Q M_g recovers it.

Conditioning on a statistic, and conditioning on any invertible function of that statistic, are the same operation: they condition on the same event. If f is injective on the attainable values of (M_1,\dots,M_Q), then \{(M_1,\dots,M_Q) = \mathrm{obs}\} and \{f(M_1,\dots,M_Q) = f(\mathrm{obs})\} are literally the same set. So the conditional distribution of anything is identical whichever way it is written (Lehmann and Romano 2005, ch. 2; this is the same reasoning that lets one condition on “the sample total” or “the sample mean” interchangeably). So: \begin{aligned} \Pr\nolimits_\beta\big(T&=t \mid M_1=M_1^{\mathrm{obs}},\dots,M_Q=M_Q^{\mathrm{obs}}\big) \;=\;\\ \Pr\nolimits_\beta\big(T&=t \mid M_{\mathrm{total}}=M_{\mathrm{total}}^{\mathrm{obs}},\ M_2=M_2^{\mathrm{obs}},\dots,M_Q=M_Q^{\mathrm{obs}}\big). \end{aligned} \qquad\text{(4.1)} The left side is what any algorithm in this package computes when G is the only thing passed as strata=. The right side is what it would compute if G were instead the only thing adjusted for. In this narrow case, the two are provably the same conditional distribution: the same exact p-value, the same exact confidence interval, the same conditional MLE.

4.3 The general principle: crossing variables into a stratification means adjusting for their full joint interaction (precisely defined)

Section 4.1 covered a single variable G with nothing else in the model. This section states the general version, for any number of variables considered jointly, and fixes precisely what “the variables” and “the full set of interaction dummy columns among them” mean, as promised at the start of Section 4. Every symbol below is defined before it is used.

Setup and notation. Let V_1,\dots,V_k denote any set of categorical variables that are being stratified jointly: that is, strata = c("V1", ..., "Vk") in the package. This works whichever way the variables arose. They might be a brand-new set of stratifiers introduced together (for example, stratifying by age, gender, and region all at once, in a model that had no strata before), or an existing set of strata (V_1,\dots,V_{k-1}, already in the model) with one further variable V_k now being added to them. The statement below does not care which; it is about the set \{V_1,\dots,V_k\} taken together as the thing being crossed into one joint stratification.

Define the composite (crossed) variable G^\star as the categorical variable whose levels are every combination of (V_1,\dots,V_k) that actually occurs in the data. If V_1,\dots,V_k have L_1,\dots,L_k levels respectively, G^\star has up to L_1\times\cdots\times L_k levels (fewer if some combinations are empty). “Stratify jointly by V_1,\dots,V_k” means, exactly, stratify by the single variable G^\star: one free intercept per combination of (V_1,\dots,V_k) that occurs, with no relationship of any kind assumed between the intercepts of different combinations.

The precise statement. Apply Section 4.1’s Model A/Model B argument with G := G^\star. Model A is “stratify by G^\star” (one free intercept per combination: this is exactly strata = c("V1",...,"Vk")). Model B is “adjust for G^\star alone,” meaning: one shared global intercept, plus a reference-coded dummy column for every combination of (V_1,\dots,V_k) that occurs, except one reference combination. Sections 4.1-4.2 apply without any change (they never used anything about G except that it is a single categorical variable), so:

Stratifying jointly by V_1,\dots,V_k is an exact reparametrisation of adjusting for one global intercept plus the full set of dummy columns for the crossed variable G^\star = V_1\times\cdots\times V_k.

This is what “the full set of interaction dummy columns among those variables” means, precisely: dummy-coding the single composite variable G^\star built by crossing all of V_1,\dots,V_k together, referenced against one baseline combination, not each V_j’s own main-effect dummies considered separately. A single set of G^\star dummy columns automatically carries every V_j’s main effect and every interaction among them (all pairwise interactions, all three-way interactions, and so on up to the full k-way interaction) as one indivisible block. There is no way to keep some of that structure and drop the rest and still have the same reparametrisation. Section 4.1 is the k=1 case of this statement, where there is only one variable and so no interaction terms to speak of. That is exactly why the distinction between “main effect” and “full interaction” never came up there.

4.4 Worked contrast: why fit23 and fit232 disagree

Section 4.3 makes it possible to say exactly why the two calls below produce different results, and to measure the difference. Take V_1= age (4 levels) and V_2= gender (2 levels) as the pre-existing strata (so R = 4\times 2 = 8 age\timesgender combinations), and V_3= region as the variable being added (Q=4 levels, so Q-1=3 main-effect dummies with region 1 as reference).

fit23 <- ep_multi_shift(
  formula = cases ~ group + region, strata = c("age","gender"),
  exact_vars = "group", ...
)   # region as a main-effect adjustment, nested in 8 age x gender strata

fit232 <- ep_multi_shift(
  formula = cases ~ group, strata = c("age","gender","region"),
  exact_vars = "group", ...
)   # age, gender, and region stratified jointly: 32 age x gender x region strata

fit232 stratifies jointly by V_1,V_2,V_3 together. By Section 4.3 this is the exact reparametrisation of one global intercept plus the full set of dummy columns for G^\star = \text{age}\times\text{gender}\times\text{region}: that is, R\times Q - 1 = 32-1=31 dummy columns, encoding the age main effect, the gender main effect, the region main effect, the age\timesgender interaction, the age\timesregion interaction, the gender\timesregion interaction, and the age\timesgender\timesregion three-way interaction, all at once. Equivalently, as fit232 actually computes it: 32 freely-varying stratum intercepts, one per combination, with \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}} built by conditioning on all 32 individual cell totals.

fit23, by contrast, has only R + (Q-1) = 8 + 3 = 11 free nuisance parameters: the 8 existing age\timesgender intercepts (which fully account for the age main effect, the gender main effect, and their mutual interaction, per Section 4.1 applied to the composite age\timesgender variable), plus region’s 3 main-effect dummies, held fixed across all 8 strata. That last part is the restriction: fit23 assumes region’s effect on the log-rate is exactly the same number in every one of the 8 age\timesgender strata. It contains no age\timesregion, gender\timesregion, or age\timesgender\timesregion terms at all.

Comparing counts directly: 11 free parameters in fit23 versus 32 in fit232, a difference of 21 parameters. That number is not arbitrary. It is exactly (R-1)(Q-1) = 7\times 3 = 21, the standard degrees of freedom for the interaction term in an R\times Q factorial layout. fit23 is fit232 with precisely that (R-1)(Q-1)-dimensional interaction block assumed away. So fit23 is a genuine sub-model of fit232, a real, testable statistical restriction, not just a relabelling. The equivalence of Sections 4.1-4.2 requires matching parameter counts on both sides, and that simply does not hold between fit23 and fit232.

The same conclusion follows directly from the sufficient statistics. fit23 conditions on 8 age-by-gender totals plus 3 global region totals (summed across all 8 strata): 11 numbers, matching its 11 free parameters. fit232 conditions on all 32 individual age-by-gender-by-region cell totals. The 32 cell totals determine the 11 coarser numbers (each is a sum of some of the 32 cells), but the reverse is false, exactly as row and column totals of a contingency table do not determine its individual cell counts. fit232 therefore conditions on strictly more information, and conditioning on more detailed information can, and generally will, shift the resulting conditional distribution of group’s sufficient statistic. That is exactly why the two commands give different answers. This is not a failure of Sections 4.1-4.2: those sections proved an equivalence for a case (a single variable, or a full joint crossing matched by full joint adjustment) that simply does not cover fit23 versus fit232, since fit23 never includes the 21 interaction dummy columns that would have made it match.

4.5 Other conditions the equivalence needs

Even in the settings covered by Sections 4.1 and 4.3, a few further conditions are worth stating explicitly:

  • The composite variable’s levels (G in Section 4.1, G^\star in Section 4.3) must be the stratum partition exactly. A continuous covariate that has been grouped into bins is different: adjusting for the bins conditions on the bin totals, which is a different sufficient statistic from adjusting for the covariate on its original continuous scale (a mode of adjustment this package does not implement at all; see Section 2.3).
  • The layout must be saturated: one free parameter per level (Section 4.1) or per combination (Section 4.3), with nothing shared or borrowed across them. A model that shares information across levels (smoothed, penalized, or otherwise constrained) is a different model, with different sufficient statistics, and the equivalence does not apply to it.

Within these conditions, the equivalence is exact, not approximate. It is a direct consequence of sufficiency being unchanged by invertible reparametrisation (Section 4.2), with no large-sample approximation anywhere in the argument.

4.6 Why the package still treats stratification and adjustment as different mechanisms

Given Sections 4.1-4.2, one might ask why the package bothers to offer strata= as a separate argument at all, rather than having users dummy-code everything into the adjustment side of the formula. The reason is computational cost, not statistical validity. The answer can be identical (in the narrow case where it applies), but the cost of getting there is not, and the difference is large enough to matter, for every algorithm in this package.

Stratification is enforced locally, at no cost to the size of the tracked table. In the dynamic program shared by Sections 5 and 7, the constraint \sum_{i\in I_s} y_i = M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} is enforced simply by keeping only the bucket m=M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} at the end of stratum s’s own pass. This is bookkeeping entirely internal to that one stratum’s loop, and it adds nothing to the (t,\mathbf{c}) key carried through the cross-stratum combination step (Section 5.4). Whether there are 2 strata or 2,000, stratification alone never changes the dimensionality of the joint coefficient table’s key. It only changes how many small per-stratum contributions need to be combined.

Adjustment is enforced globally, and adds a dimension to every tracked key. If the same Q-level variable were instead folded into X_N as Q-1 dummy columns, the adjustment machinery would need to carry Q-1 extra axes through every stratum’s computation and through the entire cross-stratum combination step, applying Rules A and B (Section 5.5) on all of them, and only filtering down to one observed combination at the very end (Section 5.6). This is exactly the “extra nuisance dimension” cost discussed in Section 10.

In practice, this means strata can be far finer than adjustment covariates ever could be. Because stratification is free in table dimensionality, every algorithm in this package handles a design stratified down to one observation per treatment arm per stratum (an individually matched design, with almost as many strata as observations) just as easily as it handles a handful of coarse strata. The per-stratum computation is trivial, and combining strata just means combining more (very small) contributions. Encoding that same fine partition as adjustment dummy columns instead would be computationally hopeless, since the coefficient table would need an axis for nearly every observation. This is why exact conditional regression methods offer stratification as a distinct mechanism from covariate adjustment (Hirji, Mehta and Patel 1987; Mehta and Patel 1995), and it is why SAS’s PROC GENMOD EXACT statement, whose cap and elimination rules this package follows (Section 5.2), likewise treats a STRATA statement as separate from the CLASS/model-effect covariates entering the EXACT list.

4.7 Choosing between stratification and adjustment in practice: a clinical-trials perspective

Sections 4.1-4.6 settle the mathematics: when the two mechanisms coincide, when they don’t, and what they cost computationally. They do not say which one a given covariate should get in a given analysis. That is a statistical modelling choice, not a fact about the algorithm, and it deserves its own guidance.

What each mechanism assumes. Stratifying a covariate gives it a fully free, unstructured effect: one parameter per level (or, jointly, per combination, Section 4.3), with nothing assumed about how levels relate to each other, and that parameter is eliminated entirely rather than estimated. Choose this when the covariate’s own effect is not of interest and there is no wish to assume anything about its shape. Adjusting for a covariate instead imposes structure: typically a single coefficient, or a small shared set of dummy coefficients, applied identically everywhere else in the model. This borrows information across levels and estimates the covariate’s own effect, but only under the assumption that a shared, simple form actually holds (linear on the log-rate scale, or one constant multiplicative shift per level, the same in every existing stratum).

Randomization stratification factors. Variables that were literally used to stratify the randomization (disease stage, prior therapy, region, sometimes site) are conventionally carried into the primary analysis as strata, not as adjustment covariates. This reflects the trial’s design, not just computational convenience: regulatory guidance on trial statistics (for example, ICH E9(R1)) ties the analysis to the randomization scheme it was built for. Treating a randomization factor as a stratum lets its baseline rate differ arbitrarily by level, with no assumption about how, say, region A relates to region B. This is appropriate when standard-of-care or population differences are expected, but there is no wish to model that relationship explicitly.

Continuous or many-level prognostic covariates. Baseline severity scores, biomarker levels, age, and similar variables are, in principle, best handled by adjusting for them as covariates on their original continuous scale rather than by stratifying. Binning a continuous variable into strata discards information, and in a trial of modest size it creates many strata with few events each, some contributing almost nothing once conditioned on. As noted in Section 2.3, however, this package’s exact-conditional implementation only supports categorical effects, so a continuous covariate must first be grouped into a small number of ordered categories before it can be stratified on or adjusted for. That grouping step reintroduces the information loss just described, and is a real, separate limitation to weigh against the assumptions discussed here, not a property of stratification versus adjustment as such.

Once a continuous covariate has been binned, though, it is just an ordinary categorical variable, and the choice of what to do with those bins is governed by exactly the same rules already given in this section, with no special case for the fact that the categories originated from a continuous scale: Sections 4.1-4.3’s stratify/adjust equivalence, Section 4.6’s cost trade-off, and the bias-variance and interaction guidance above all apply to the binned variable directly. To be concrete about what this package recommends in practice: prefer as few bins as the clinical question allows: established, pre-specified clinical cutpoints if they exist (for example, a standard severity-score threshold), or otherwise tertiles or quartiles of the observed data, rather than many narrow bins, since each additional bin is either an extra stratum (more sparsely-populated strata, Section 4.6) or an extra adjustment dummy (more nuisance columns, at the cost described in Section 4.6). Adjust for the binned covariate (rather than stratifying on it) unless there is a specific reason to think its association with the outcome differs across levels of the effect under test, in which case stratifying jointly with it, per Section 4.4’s worked contrast, is the honest choice.

Stratifying costs nothing in table dimensionality in this package’s exact-conditional algorithms (Section 4.6), but it still costs information statistically: each stratum’s contribution to inference comes only from the observations inside it. Many strata with sparse events mean a lot of unshared, individually estimated structure. Adjustment assumes commonality across strata up front, which is more efficient when that assumption holds and biased when it does not.

Section 4.4’s worked contrast is the sharpest version of this trade-off. Stratifying a covariate jointly with existing strata (fit232-style) lets its effect vary completely freely across every existing stratum. Adjusting for it as a covariate nested inside existing strata (fit23-style) assumes its effect is the same constant everywhere. If there is reason to think a covariate’s association with the outcome genuinely differs across levels of another factor already in the model (a treatment-by-region interaction, say), stratifying jointly (or explicitly fitting interaction terms) is the honest choice. Treating it as a plain, main-effect-only adjustment covariate is only valid to the extent that interaction can reasonably be ruled out, and Section 4.4 shows concretely how large a restriction that assumption is: (R-1)(Q-1) degrees of freedom of interaction structure, assumed away.

5. The multivariate-shift algorithm (ep_multi_shift())

This algorithm computes C(t) for any number of categorical covariates (any number of nuisance columns p \ge 0) and any number of strata, following the conventions of SAS PROC GENMOD’s EXACT statement. It is the multivariate-shift algorithm: a per-stratum dynamic program combined with explicit cross-stratum convolution. It adapts ideas from Hirji, Mehta and Patel (1987), originally built for exact logistic regression where every y_i \in \{0,1\}, to Poisson counts bounded by SAS-style caps. (This is distinct from SAS’s own METHOD=NETWORK, described in Section 7, which prunes continuously, observation by observation, rather than building an explicit joint table per stratum.)

5.1 The Poisson base measure, explicitly

Section 3.1 stated this compactly; here is the full derivation. The Poisson pmf \Pr(Y_i=y_i\mid\mu_i) = \mu_i^{y_i}e^{-\mu_i}/y_i! gives, using (2.1), \prod_i \Pr(Y_i=y_i\mid\mu_i) = \prod_i \frac{\big(E_i\,e^{\tau_{s(i)}+\beta z_i+\boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{x}_{N,i}}\big)^{y_i}}{y_i!}\, e^{-E_i e^{\tau_{s(i)}+\beta z_i+\boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{x}_{N,i}}}. Every factor e^{y_i(\tau_{s(i)}+\beta z_i + \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{x}_{N,i})} contributes to the canonical linear form (3.1). Everything else (E_i^{y_i}/y_i! and the normalizing exponential) either does not depend on the parameters, or is constant given the conditioning statistics. Collecting the parameter-free part defines the base measure w(y) := \prod_i E_i^{y_i}/y_i!, with \log w(y) = \sum_i(y_i o_i - \log(y_i!)): exactly the quantity accumulated by the dynamic program below.

5.2 SAS-style cap rules for S_i

Three mutually exclusive rules set the per-observation cap S_i, matching SAS’s OFFSET/EXACTMAX conventions exactly:

  1. EXACTMAX = var specified. S_i = e_i, the observed value of the supplied variable, per observation.
  2. EXACTMAX specified without a variable, or neither OFFSET nor EXACTMAX specified. There is nothing else to bound y_i by, so the procedure uses the intercept’s own sufficient statistic within the observation’s stratum: S_i = M_{s(i)}^{\mathrm{obs}} (single stratum: S_i = M^{\mathrm{obs}} for everyone).
  3. OFFSET specified, EXACTMAX not specified. S_i = \max\!\big(\lceil e^{o_i}\rceil,\ 1\big), with the feasibility requirement S_i \ge y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}.

These three rules are not all the same kind of restriction, and it is worth being precise about that. Rule 2’s cap is implied by conditioning alone; it is not an extra assumption. If \sum_{j \in I_s} y_j = M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} and every y_j \ge 0, then for any single i \in I_s, y_i = M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} - \sum_{j\ne i} y_j \le M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} automatically. The stratum-total conditioning event already forces 0 \le y_i \le M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} with no further assumption. So Rule 2’s cap simply restates a bound that was already there. (Concretely, the per-observation loop bound in Section 5.3, \min(S_i,\ M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}-m), reduces to M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}-m under Rule 2, since S_i = M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} \ge M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}-m whenever m\ge0.) Rules 1 and 3, by contrast, are genuine additional modelling assumptions, adopted for tractability and to match SAS’s own convention (SAS Institute, SAS/STAT User’s Guide, the GENMOD procedure’s EXACT statement). They assert that individual counts above a stated bound (a known capacity e_i, or a bound implied by the observation’s own exposure) are a priori impossible. Conditioning does not give that assumption for free; it would need to be justified on subject-matter grounds in any given application. First rule only restates what was already true, second and third rules genuinely narrow the reference set further. That is exactly why the cap rules are documented as rules the package resolves automatically from what was supplied, not a single automatic default and not something a user tunes directly.

These three rules, and only these three, determine \mathcal{B}(Q) and hence \Omega and \Omega_{\mathrm{cond}} (Section 3.3). In the code, this logic lives in parse_exactmax_spec(), si_from_exactmax_var(), si_from_stratum_total(), and si_from_offset(). The choice among the three rules is made once, automatically, from whether exactmax/offset were supplied. There is no argument for substituting a different rule.

5.3 Stratum-level decomposition and the within-stratum dynamic program

Strata are disjoint, and both the base measure and the sufficient statistics factor (or add) across strata, so the problem decomposes stratum by stratum. Write y_s = (y_i)_{i \in I_s} and, restricted to stratum s, define w_s(y_s) := \prod_{i \in I_s} \frac{E_i^{y_i}}{y_i!}, \qquad T_s(y_s) := \sum_{i \in I_s} y_i z_i, \qquad \mathbf{T}_{N,s}(y_s) := \sum_{i \in I_s} y_i\, \mathbf{x}_{N,i}, \Omega_s := \Big\{\, y_s \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{|I_s|} : \sum_{i \in I_s} y_i = M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}, \ 0 \le y_i \le S_i \,\Big\}, C_s(t_s, \mathbf{c}_s \mid M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}) := \sum_{y_s \in \Omega_s} \mathbf{1}\{T_s(y_s)=t_s,\ \mathbf{T}_{N,s}(y_s)=\mathbf{c}_s\}\, w_s(y_s). Each stratum’s coefficient table C_s is built by a dynamic program that processes that stratum’s observations one at a time, keeping track of:

  • buckets, indexed by the partial stratum total m = 0, 1, \dots, M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} accumulated so far;
  • within each bucket, a (sparse) map from the key (t, \mathbf{c}) (the partial values of the interest and nuisance statistics) to a log coefficient (the natural log of the accumulated base-measure weight, kept in log scale for numerical stability).

When processing observation i: for every current bucket m and every feasible increment yy \in \{0,\dots,\min(S_i,\ M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}-m)\}, the recursion moves probability mass from bucket m to bucket m+yy, updates the key by t \mathrel{+}= yy\, z_i and \mathbf{c} \mathrel{+}= yy\, \mathbf{x}_{N,i}, and adds the log-weight increment yy\, o_i - \log(yy!) (the log of E_i^{yy}/yy!, the i-th factor of w_s). States landing on the same key within a bucket are merged by log-sum-exp (Section 9). After the last observation of the stratum, only the bucket m = M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} is kept: this is exactly what enforces the stratum-total constraint that defines \Omega_s. In the code this recursion is .joint_dist_stratum_dp_vec() (ep-multivariate-shift.R), implemented directly as a vectorized base-R operation: a row-replication-and-grouping step over plain named lists of vectors, rather than a nested per-value loop (Section 5.8 gives the engineering detail).

5.4 Combining strata (convolution)

Statistics add and weights multiply across strata (they are independent given the stratum totals), so the global joint table is the multi-dimensional convolution of the per-stratum tables: C(t,\mathbf{c}) = \sum_{\substack{(t_1,\dots,t_Q):\ \sum_s t_s = t \\ (\mathbf{c}_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}_Q):\ \sum_s \mathbf{c}_s = \mathbf{c}}} \ \prod_{s=1}^Q C_s(t_s,\mathbf{c}_s \mid M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}). \qquad\text{(5.1)} This is computed by repeated pairwise convolution. Start from the first stratum’s table (Section 5.7 fixes the processing order), and combine it, one stratum at a time, with each remaining stratum’s table. For every pair of keys \big((t_1,\mathbf{c}_1),(t_2,\mathbf{c}_2)\big), one from each table, form the new key (t_1+t_2,\ \mathbf{c}_1+\mathbf{c}_2) and the new log-weight (the sum of the two), then merge duplicate resulting keys by log-sum-exp. In the code, .convolve_joint_pnuis_vec() performs this pairwise convolution in row-chunks (size set by chunk_size), to bound peak memory when both tables being combined are large.

5.5 Pruning for feasibility (Rule A and Rule B)

The joint table grows with every nuisance axis and can get large. Two safe pruning rules discard states that provably cannot reach the observed nuisance total, and never discard a state that could still be needed. Both rules are valid whenever every nuisance increment is non-negative, which is the usual case for 0/1 dummy columns and non-negative counts:

  • Rule A (upper-bound pruning). For each nuisance component k: if the partial value c_k already exceeds the observed total t_{N,\mathrm{obs},k}, discard the state. Non-negative increments mean nuisance totals never decrease as more strata or observations are added, so overshooting can never be corrected later.
  • Rule B (reachability pruning). For stratum s and nuisance component k, define the per-stratum upper bound on how much that stratum alone could still add (Section 2.5’s U_{s,k}), U_{s,k} := \min\!\Big(M_s^{\mathrm{obs}},\ \sum_{i \in I_s:\ x_{ik}\ne 0} S_i\Big), and, once some initial strata have already been combined, the total remaining upper bound U^{\mathrm{rem}}_k := \sum_{\text{strata not yet processed}} U_{r,k}. A partial state with nuisance value c_k is discarded if c_k + U^{\mathrm{rem}}_k < t_{N,\mathrm{obs},k}: even the best possible outcome from every remaining stratum could not reach the observed total. (Section 2.5 explains why M_s^{\mathrm{obs}} appearing inside this formula does not make it k-indexed in its own right.)

Both rules are exact: they never remove a state that belongs in the final answer. They are applied directly inside the per-stratum recursion (Rule A, via the tN_obs cap) and inside the combination step (Rule B, via remaining_max in .convolve_joint_pnuis_vec()). Every stratum’s own table C_s is built regardless of processing order (step 4 below). So once all Q tables exist, their exact row counts are known at no extra cost. Strata are then always combined smallest-table-first (ordering by nrow() of each stratum’s own table, automatically, not a user-configurable option), because this keeps the running accumulator as small as possible for as long as possible, and makes Rule B’s bound tightest early, when it matters most. A table’s row count, not the stratum’s raw observed total M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}, is used for this ordering because it is the quantity that actually determines combination cost, and it is available for free here. Contrast this with ep_network() (Section 7.6), which never builds a per-stratum table at all and must therefore fall back to the cheaper (but less exact) proxy M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}, decided before any per-stratum work begins.

5.6 Filtering and marginalizing to C(t)

After the full combination over all Q strata, one joint table C(t,\mathbf{c}) remains. Two final steps produce the one-dimensional table needed for inference. First, filter to the observed nuisance value (keep only rows with \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}}). Then marginalize: drop the now-constant nuisance key, summing via log-sum-exp any duplicate t values left over: C(t) = C(t, \mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}}). This is filter_and_marginalize_pn_lw() in the code. Its output, the pairs \{(t, \log C(t))\}, is exactly the one-dimensional table Section 8 uses for every exact-inference quantity.

5.7 Algorithmic summary: the exact steps performed

For each requested effect (a single model-matrix column \mathbf{z}) in exact_vars, ep_multi_shift() performs:

  1. Resolve the caps S_i for every observation, using whichever of the three rules in Section 5.2 applies (EXACTMAX=var, EXACTMAX without a variable / no offset, or OFFSET alone).
  2. Build the model matrix, identify the column \mathbf{z} for the current effect, and identify the nuisance columns X_N: either every other model-matrix column (condition_on = "model", the SAS-matching default) or only the other requested exact effects (condition_on = "exact").
  3. Compute the observed nuisance total \mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}} = X_N^\top y^{\mathrm{obs}} and the observed interest statistic t_{\mathrm{obs}} = z^\top y^{\mathrm{obs}}.
  4. For each stratum, run the within-stratum dynamic program (Section 5.3) to get that stratum’s own coefficient table C_s(t_s,\mathbf{c}_s \mid M_s^{\mathrm{obs}}), applying Rule A pruning against \mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}} as states are generated.
  5. Order the strata by ascending row count of their own just-built table (Section 5.5), and compute each stratum’s maximum possible contribution to every nuisance component, for use by Rule B.
  6. Combine the per-stratum tables pairwise, in chunks, applying Rule B pruning (using the running “remaining maximum” bound) after each stratum is folded in, to get the joint table C(t,\mathbf{c}).
  7. Filter the joint table to \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{t}_{N,\mathrm{obs}} and marginalize to the one-dimensional table \{(t,\log C(t))\}_{t\in\mathcal{T}}.
  8. Compute exact inference from this one table: the conditional MLE, the exact confidence interval, and the exact p-value (Section 8), and record the parameter’s row of exactparmest and its distribution in OUTDIST.
  9. Repeat steps 2-8 for every remaining requested effect.

6. The closed-form algorithm (ep_closed_form())

6.1 The special case

ep_closed_form() targets one specific, very common special case of the general model: exactly one two-level (treatment vs. control) effect of interest, with strata as the only other structure in the model (no additional categorical covariates to adjust for: p = 0, no X_N at all). This is the classical setting of Guess, Lydick, Small and Miller (1987) and Guess and Thomas (1990): a stratified comparison of two incidence rates from person-time data.

For stratum s = 1,\dots,Q, let y_s^{(1)}, y_s^{(0)} be the observed event counts in the treatment and control groups (aggregated within the stratum), and e_s^{(1)}, e_s^{(0)} the corresponding exposures (person-time). The model is Y_s^{(1)} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(e_s^{(1)} \lambda_s \theta), \qquad Y_s^{(0)} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(e_s^{(0)} \lambda_s), \qquad s=1,\dots,Q, equivalently \log\mathbb{E}[Y_s^{(1)}] = \log e_s^{(1)} + \log\lambda_s + \beta, \log\mathbb{E}[Y_s^{(0)}] = \log e_s^{(0)} + \log\lambda_s, \beta := \log\theta, where \lambda_s > 0 is a stratum-specific nuisance baseline rate and \theta > 0 is the rate ratio. \theta carries no stratum index s, exactly as Guess and Thomas (1990) state it in their own model formulation (“the relative risk \omega = r_{1i}/r_{0i} is assumed to be constant across strata,” their notation for this section’s \theta and s). This is exactly the general model of Section 2.4, with the offset o_i = \log e_s^{(1)} or \log e_s^{(0)} depending on group, the stratum intercept \tau_{s(i)} = \log\lambda_s, the treatment indicator as z_i, and the nuisance design matrix X_N empty. So the “constant across strata” assumption here is not a simplification specific to this closed-form special case. It is the same assumption Section 2.4 already makes for \beta in the fully general model, together with the observation there that a fully free, stratum-specific \lambda_s (baseline rate) does nothing to relax it: \lambda_s is free to differ arbitrarily from stratum to stratum, while \theta, the ratio on top of it, is assumed to be the same number everywhere. Like every other function in this package, the exposure/offset is optional: if none is supplied, every observation is treated as contributing one unit of exposure (o_i = 0).

6.2 Deriving the within-stratum conditional distribution (Poisson thinning)

The nuisance parameter here is \lambda_s, and its sufficient statistic is the stratum total T_s := Y_s^{(1)} + Y_s^{(0)}. Y_s^{(1)} and Y_s^{(0)} are independent Poisson variables, so their sum is Poisson too, with the rates added: T_s = Y_s^{(1)} + Y_s^{(0)} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\big(e_s^{(1)}\lambda_s\theta + e_s^{(0)}\lambda_s\big). The conditional probability that Y_s^{(1)} = r (so Y_s^{(0)} = t_s-r), given T_s = t_s, is the joint probability divided by this marginal: \begin{aligned} \Pr(Y_s^{(1)}=r \mid T_s=t_s) &= \frac{\Pr(Y_s^{(1)}=r)\Pr(Y_s^{(0)}=t_s-r)}{\Pr(T_s=t_s)}\\ &= \frac{\dfrac{(e_s^{(1)}\lambda_s\theta)^r e^{-e_s^{(1)}\lambda_s\theta}}{r!}\cdot\dfrac{(e_s^{(0)}\lambda_s)^{t_s-r}e^{-e_s^{(0)}\lambda_s}}{(t_s-r)!}}{\dfrac{(e_s^{(1)}\lambda_s\theta+e_s^{(0)}\lambda_s)^{t_s}e^{-(e_s^{(1)}\lambda_s\theta+e_s^{(0)}\lambda_s)}}{t_s!}}. \end{aligned} The two exponentials in the numerator multiply to e^{-(e_s^{(1)}\lambda_s\theta+e_s^{(0)}\lambda_s)}, which cancels exactly against the denominator’s exponential. This is where \lambda_s starts to disappear (a direct, concrete instance of the general cancellation argument in Section 3.4). What remains is \begin{aligned} \Pr(Y_s^{(1)}=r\mid T_s=t_s) &= \binom{t_s}{r}\frac{(e_s^{(1)}\lambda_s\theta)^r(e_s^{(0)}\lambda_s)^{t_s-r}}{(e_s^{(1)}\lambda_s\theta+e_s^{(0)}\lambda_s)^{t_s}}\\ &= \binom{t_s}{r}\left(\frac{e_s^{(1)}\theta}{e_s^{(1)}\theta+e_s^{(0)}}\right)^{\!r}\left(\frac{e_s^{(0)}}{e_s^{(1)}\theta+e_s^{(0)}}\right)^{\!t_s-r}, \end{aligned} \qquad\text{(6.1)} Every remaining factor of \lambda_s has also cancelled, leaving an expression that depends only on the data and \theta. This is exactly \mathrm{Binomial}(t_s,\ p_s(\theta)), with p_s(\theta) := \frac{e_s^{(1)}\theta}{e_s^{(1)}\theta+e_s^{(0)}}. Conditioning on the stratum total does two things at once. It removes \lambda_s completely (guaranteed in general by Section 3.2, since T_s is \lambda_s’s sufficient statistic), and it leaves behind a Binomial count, which is simple enough to have a closed-form generating function. The general theorem (Section 3.2) guarantees the conditional distribution is free of \lambda_s, but it does not, by itself, guarantee that distribution will be simple; that extra convenience is Poisson-specific. Independence across strata follows because \big(Y_1^{(1)},\dots,Y_Q^{(1)}\big) given (T_1,\dots,T_Q) factors into the product of these Q conditional distributions.

6.3 The coefficient table as a polynomial in \theta

Writing (6.1) as a function of \theta, \Pr(Y_s^{(1)}=r\mid T_s=t_s) = \left(\frac{e_s^{(0)}}{e_s^{(1)}\theta+e_s^{(0)}}\right)^{\!t_s}\binom{t_s}{r}\left(\frac{e_s^{(1)}}{e_s^{(0)}}\right)^{\!r}\theta^r, the prefactor does not depend on r. All of the dependence on which value Y_s^{(1)} takes is carried by \binom{t_s}{r}(e_s^{(1)}/e_s^{(0)})^r\theta^r: the r-th term of the binomial expansion of \big(1+\tfrac{e_s^{(1)}}{e_s^{(0)}}\theta\big)^{t_s}. Conditional on every T_s, the whole-sample sufficient statistic K := \sum_{s=1}^Q Y_s^{(1)} is a sum of independent (though not identically distributed) Binomial counts. Its distribution as a function of \theta therefore comes from multiplying the Q per-stratum polynomials and reading off the coefficient of \theta^k: c_k = \sum_{\substack{r_1+\cdots+r_Q=k \\ 0\le r_s\le t_s}}\ \prod_{s=1}^Q \binom{t_s}{r_s}\left(\frac{e_s^{(1)}}{e_s^{(0)}}\right)^{r_s}, \qquad \Pr\nolimits_\theta(K=k) = \left[\prod_{s=1}^Q\left(\frac{e_s^{(0)}}{e_s^{(1)}\theta+e_s^{(0)}}\right)^{t_s}\right] c_k\,\theta^k. \qquad\text{(6.2)} Normalizing (6.2) over k removes the bracketed factor, since it does not depend on k. This leaves the same exponential-tilt form as the general algorithm (equation 3.3): \Pr\nolimits_\theta(K=k) = \frac{c_k\,\theta^k}{\sum_u c_u\,\theta^u}, \qquad \beta = \log\theta. \qquad\text{(6.3)} Combining strata is therefore literally multiplying Q polynomials of degree t_1,\dots,t_Q: a one-dimensional convolution of vectors of length t_s+1, computed stratum by stratum by an accumulate-and-merge recursion (compute_ck_natlog() in the code, working with natural-log coefficients \log c_k throughout, purely for numerical stability, with no change to the mathematics above). Section 6.3.1 gives that recursion in full, together with the specific bound that makes it fast.

6.3.1 The Guess-Thomas (1990) recursive algorithm, and why it is fast

A local notation note before starting. To match Guess and Thomas’s (1990) own presentation, this subsection indexes strata by i=1,\dots,Q (so “stratum i,” “the first i strata”) rather than this document’s usual stratum letter s. This i is scoped entirely to this subsection and never refers to an individual observation, unlike every other use of i elsewhere in this document (Section 2.1). Similarly, L_i and H_i below are local summation bounds specific to this recursion, unrelated to the per-stratum bounds L_{s,k} and U_{s,k} of Section 2.5/5.5; both pairs happen to use the letters L and U/H for a similar purpose (bracketing a sum), but they are otherwise different quantities defined for different purposes, and neither is used again outside its own subsection.

Equation (6.2) could in principle be evaluated by expanding the polynomial product directly, one stratum at a time, tracking every coefficient up to the full degree \sum_s t_s at every intermediate stage. That direct approach is exactly the original algorithm of Guess, Lydick, Small, and Miller (1987), and its running time grows like T^Q (T the largest stratum total, Q the number of strata). This is fine for a handful of small strata, but prohibitive once either grows. Guess and Thomas (1990) instead adapt the network-based recursive-convolution technique that Mehta and Patel had already developed for related exact-inference problems (Mehta and Patel 1983; Mehta, Patel, and Gray 1985) to this specific binomial-thinning setting. This gives an algorithm with the same theoretical definitions and the same numerical answers as the 1987 method, but a running time that grows only like (ST)^2. On their own worked example (a table with six non-null strata and 37 cases), the direct method took several hours on the hardware of the time, against about 50 seconds for the recursive method: better than a hundredfold speed-up on that example, and the method this package’s own compute_ck_natlog() implements.

Define M(0,0) := 1 and, for stratum i=1,\dots,Q, the partial coefficient table built from the first i strata alone, \begin{aligned} M(i,k) &:= \big[\theta^k\big]\prod_{s=1}^i\left(1+\frac{e_s^{(1)}}{e_s^{(0)}}\theta\right)^{t_s} \\ &= \sum_{\substack{j_1+\cdots+j_i=k\\ 0\le j_s\le t_s}}\ \prod_{s=1}^i \binom{t_s}{j_s}\left(\frac{e_s^{(1)}}{e_s^{(0)}}\right)^{j_s} \qquad\text{so that}\qquad c_k = M(Q,k). \end{aligned}, M(i,k) satisfies the one-stratum-at-a-time recursion obtained by multiplying in stratum i’s own polynomial, M(i,k) = \sum_{r=L_i}^{H_i} M(i-1,\ k-r)\, \binom{t_i}{r}\left(\frac{e_i^{(1)}}{e_i^{(0)}}\right)^{r}, \qquad L_i := \max\big(0,\ k-V_{i-1}\big), \quad H_i := \min\big(k,\ t_i\big), where V_i := \min\!\big(N,\ \sum_{s=1}^i t_s\big) and V_0 := 0. Here N denotes how far the table actually needs to be built for the purpose at hand: it is not a fixed constant, but whichever of the following two values the caller actually needs: the observed total k_{\mathrm{obs}} = \sum_s y_s^{(1)} for the truncated table used by the p-value and confidence interval (Section 6.5), or the full \sum_s t_s for the complete table the conditional MLE needs (Section 8.2). This recursion computes exactly the same c_k as the direct expansion of (6.2). It is the identical polynomial multiplication, one stratum at a time, with one addition: at every intermediate stage i, only coefficients k \le V_i are ever computed or stored. This is a safe truncation. It never discards a coefficient the final table could still need, because every stratum’s contribution to k is non-negative: a partial total already above N can never be brought back down to N or below by any later stratum, so it can never contribute to a final coefficient c_k with k\le N. Bounding the table’s width by N at every stage, rather than letting it grow with the full (and possibly much larger) \sum_{s\le i} t_s, is the entire source of the (ST)^2 speed-up over the 1987 method’s T^Q. The two algorithms compute the identical sequence of polynomial multiplications; they differ only in how much of each intermediate result is worth keeping.

compute_ck_natlog() implements this recursion directly and by name. vvi <- pmin(max_cases, cumsum(t)) is exactly V_i for every stratum at once (with max_cases the caller-supplied N, max_k in the function’s own argument list, Section 6.5), and its nested loop over k and then r is exactly M(i,k)’s own sum over r=L_i,\dots,H_i. Guess and Thomas (1990) note that the terms M(i,k), c_k, and c_k\theta^k are prone to the same overflow and underflow difficulties as the analogous terms in Mehta and Patel’s own network algorithms, and they handle them the same way: every one of these quantities is carried on the natural-log scale, with any sum of two log-scale terms computed via the log-sum-exp identity (Section 9) rather than by exponentiating and re-summing directly. compute_ck_natlog() follows this exactly, hence its name, and hence why every quantity in this section is written on the log scale throughout.

6.4 Correspondence with the general coefficient table

c_k above is exactly the general coefficient table C(t,\mathbf{c}) of Section 3.4, specialized to p=0 (no nuisance columns at all), with a per-observation cap S_i equal to the stratum total: precisely SAS’s own Rule 2 (Section 5.2) for eliminating stratum intercepts. ep_closed_form() has no exactmax argument, and its derivation above (Sections 6.1-6.2) conditions only on the stratum total T_s: there is no place in it for a per-observation cap at all. So this function always uses Rule 2, regardless of whether offset is supplied to the call. This is unlike the two general algorithms (Sections 5 and 7), which switch automatically to Rule 3’s offset-implied cap whenever offset is supplied without exactmax (Section 5.2). That difference is not just cosmetic: when Rule 3’s cap would actually bind, the closed-form algorithm and the two general algorithms are constraining \Omega differently and can legitimately disagree (Section 10). Where the caps coincide (no offset, or an offset too generous to bind), every algorithm in this package eliminates stratum intercepts the same way: a per-stratum sub-computation constrained to that stratum’s own total, followed by combining strata. (Compare Sections 5.3-5.4 and Sections 7.2-7.6 directly with Sections 6.2-6.3: they are the same operation, specialized or restructured.) With no nuisance columns to track, all of them collapse to the univariate binomial/polynomial picture above. With one or more nuisance columns, the per-stratum computation and the cross-stratum combination have to carry those extra axes along too, at a cost the closed-form algorithm never has to pay (Section 10).

6.5 Exact inference specifics: the truncated-table trick

Everything downstream follows the same pattern as the general algorithm (Section 8), applied to the one-dimensional table \{(k,c_k)\} of (6.2). One extra trick, specific to this algorithm’s reparametrisation on \beta, is worth deriving explicitly, since it accounts for much of its speed (Section 10).

\Pr_\beta(K=k) in (6.3) always sums to one over k’s complete support, at every value of \beta. That means the total normalizing constant has a closed form that never requires summing the coefficient table at all: Z(\beta) := \sum_u c_u\, e^{\beta u} = \left[\prod_{s=1}^Q\left(\frac{e_s^{(0)}}{e_s^{(1)}\theta+e_s^{(0)}}\right)^{t_s}\right]^{-1} = \prod_{s=1}^Q \left(\frac{e_s^{(1)}\theta+e_s^{(0)}}{e_s^{(0)}}\right)^{t_s}, \qquad \theta=e^\beta. Equivalently, on the log scale, with \log(1-p_\theta(s)) := \log e_s^{(0)} - \log(e_s^{(1)}\theta+e_s^{(0)}) the per-stratum log-probability of the “control” outcome, \log Z(\beta) = -\sum_{s=1}^Q t_s\,\log\big(1-p_\theta(s)\big) =: -g(\beta). So any tail probability of K (\Pr_\beta(K\le k_0) or \Pr_\beta(K\ge k_0), at any \beta, not only \beta=0) can be computed from a truncated coefficient table (only the c_k for k on the near side of k_0), plus this analytic normalizing factor, using the complement for the far side: \Pr\nolimits_\beta(K\le k_0) = \sum_{k=0}^{k_0} c_k\, e^{\beta k + g(\beta)}, \qquad \Pr\nolimits_\beta(K\ge k_0) = 1 - \Pr\nolimits_\beta(K\le k_0-1). The exact p-value and the exact confidence interval only ever need \Pr_\beta(K\le k_{\mathrm{obs}}) and \Pr_\beta(K\ge k_{\mathrm{obs}}) (Section 8). So the coefficient table only ever has to be built up to k = k_{\mathrm{obs}} for those two quantities (compute_ck_natlog(..., max_k = sum(x)), the default). Only the conditional MLE genuinely needs the mean of K over its entire range, and it is the only one that requires the complete table (max_k = sum(x) + sum(y)). This same fact (that a tail probability at any \beta can be recovered from the already-built table without re-enumerating anything) is also exactly what lets a p-value be recomputed against a different null hypothesis, or a confidence interval at a different \alpha, from a fit that has already run: see the companion vignette, vignette("Example"), for a worked example.

6.6 Why the search over \beta is done the way it is

Both the exact CI limits and the exact p-value require finding a \beta at which a tail probability (evaluated with the truncated-table-plus-analytic-normalizer formula in Section 6.5) equals a target value (for example, \alpha/2). This is a one-dimensional root-finding problem in \beta. The implementation (solve_tail_root(), shared with every other algorithm, Section 8) finds a bracket containing the root by doubling a symmetric interval around \beta=0 until the target function changes sign at its two ends, then refines the root with a standard bisection/Brent-style search (stats::uniroot()). Searching in \beta (the natural, unbounded parameter) with a sign-change-based bracket guarantees the search is mathematically valid no matter how extreme the true root is. A one-directional multiplicative bracket expansion searched directly on the rate-ratio scale \theta \in (0,\infty) can, for at least one realistic dataset, silently fail to bracket the true root and converge to a value many orders of magnitude off, because expanding the bracket in only one direction does not correctly detect that the root is actually smaller than the current guess. The \beta-scale, sign-change-based search used throughout this package does not have that failure mode.

6.7 Algorithmic summary: the exact steps performed

  1. Aggregate to per-stratum arm counts: for each stratum s, compute the four numbers (y_s^{(1)}, y_s^{(0)}, e_s^{(1)}, e_s^{(0)}) (treatment/control event counts and exposures) by summing over whichever individual rows of data fall in that stratum and that level of exact_vars. data may be individual-level or already aggregated; the summation makes the two equivalent as inputs.
  2. Build the truncated coefficient table \{(k, \log c_k)\}_{k=0}^{k_{\mathrm{obs}}} via compute_ck_natlog(), where k_{\mathrm{obs}} := \sum_s y_s^{(1)} is the observed value of the whole-sample sufficient statistic.
  3. Evaluate the two one-sided tail probabilities at \beta=0 (\Pr_0(K \le k_{\mathrm{obs}}) and \Pr_0(K \ge k_{\mathrm{obs}})) using the truncated table plus the analytic normalizing factor g(\beta) of Section 6.5, and combine them into the two-sided exact p-value (Section 8.4, shared with every other algorithm).
  4. Find the exact confidence limits by root-finding in \beta (Section 6.6): for a two-sided interval, solve \Pr_\beta(K \ge k_{\mathrm{obs}}) = \alpha/2 for the lower limit and \Pr_\beta(K \le k_{\mathrm{obs}}) = \alpha/2 for the upper limit, each using the same truncated-table trick; a limit is set to \mp\infty directly, without root-finding, if k_{\mathrm{obs}} sits at the boundary of its attainable range.
  5. Build the complete coefficient table \{(k,\log c_k)\}_{k=0}^{k_{\mathrm{obs}}+\sum_s y_s^{(0)}} (compute_ck_natlog(..., max_k = sum(x)+sum(y))) and use it to solve for the conditional MLE \hat\beta (Section 8.2, shared with every other algorithm), the one quantity that genuinely needs the whole table rather than a truncation of it.
  6. Assemble the result: one row of exactparmest (Parameter, Estimate = \hat\beta, StdError, Alpha, LowerCL, UpperCL, PValue, SuffStat = k_{\mathrm{obs}}) and one entry of OUTDIST (the complete distribution \{(k,\Pr_0(K=k))\}, for inspection or plotting, and, as Section 6.5 notes, for direct reuse afterward).
